I mean, that would be great.
Yeah, that'd be.

Obviously, I'm also kind of interested in.

Come here.

Yeah, yeah, absolutely.
I guess I can go first, intro wise.
So I'm Sarah and I lead our corporate development efforts across the UK and Europe in regards to the retail, education and travel sectors.
My role is to speak with owners of software companies and their partners that are thinking about an exit, whether it's today or further down the road.
Patti, would you like to introduce yourself?
I can kind of give the Banyan Spiel afterwards.
Yeah.
So, Patrick Connolly.
I work in the M and A investment team here at Banyan Kiwi, who has made his Way across the ditch to the UK and been with Banyan for about a year now, which seems like an eternity.
Get the speed we've been moving.
So I feel like I'm part of the furniture.
Yeah, exactly.
I guess I should say as well.

I'm originally from Canada, so I started with Banyan in our Toronto office, so that's where our largest management office is based out of, and then moved over to the UK with Banyan to help expand our presence over here just over a year ago.
Similar to Patti does feel like a long time.
But essentially Banyan as a whole, our mission is to provide the best permanent, whole, sorry, permanent home for great software companies that have dominant positions in niche markets.
So we do buy and hold our businesses for life.
We don't resell them down the road.
We generally are 100% acquirers and then we operate our businesses independently in a decentralized fashion, really preserve the legacy of the businesses for the founders and then post acquisition.
And I think this is what really makes us stand out in the buy and hold space is our focus on that long term sustainable growth.
From a portfolio perspective, we have 84 businesses within our portfolio and these are.
We're very sector agnostic.
So they span from retail, education, government, communications, transportation, manufacturing, sports and leisure, et cetera.
And then they're based primarily throughout North America.
And then as well, we've been growing quite substantially in the uk, Europe and Australia and New Zealand and.
And then across all of those portfolio companies, we're very proud to say we're 100% referenceable across all past sellers.

From a metrics perspective, typically from a USD standpoint, where we look to hire businesses between 2 to 30 million in annual turnover, with the high majority coming from recurring revenues from a profitability perspective, typically over 500k and from a growth perspective, typically we'll say over 5%, but we can be quite flexible.
And then from a gross customer return perspective, typically we'll look over 90%.
From a management perspective, each business we acquire is very unique and kind of dependent on what the founder wants.

We're very flexible in regards to if they want to leave straight away, if they're looking to stay on for five plus years and really excited to help build on the success they've created, either if they want to exit or if they want to stay on for the long term.
And then from a TGS perspective or tsg, sorry perspective, we were really excited about the business when we initially looked at it.
I mean the global market leadership is very impressive.
I think the growth the historic growth and the growth opportunities for the business were really exciting to us as well.
And then the customer base that they've cultivated was really attractive to us too.
I think at that time, from the recurring revenue standpoint, we weren't necessarily extremely comfortable with that transactional piece of the revenue and the services component within rmi.
I think since then we've become a little bit more opportunistic in what we consider recurring versus reoccurring.

And then from a customer concentration perspective, I think having the when we last looked and I think the data that we have is from July 24th, if I'm not mistaken, kind of that over 50% of customer concentration in the top five was something that kind of steered us away.

But understanding that there's been a lot of development in the pipeline and the customer base in the past four months was really exciting to hear and something that we'd be looking to discuss further.
Yeah.
Just to add on to Sarah's point, I think she's covered most of it, but the financials like at face value always stacked up for us.
And we've acquired a couple of businesses now that are either partly or fully transactional based, which was kind of how we would look at the commission component.

And given the fixed that in the contracts is a fixed component, which is what we consider recurring, we can now take a more step back, take a holistic view on the commission structure as being reoccurring and get comfort in that.
And we've worked with some partners now that have been really good at getting us comfortable where we've got customer concentration.

We, as part of our diligence process will undertake customer calls and do some really in depth market research to understand the competitive landscape which can support our investment thesis and somewhat de risk those areas as much as possible, or if not de risk, understand them.
Okay, great.
Well, thank you for the background, guys.
So I'm Andy Day of Capital A and I'm the CEO of the company.
And so I haven't met you guys before, but certainly good to get the background on it.
Yeah.
So in terms of like the changes since we last spoke, obviously it's been quite a while, but there was client concentration that actually in the interim they've lost one of their bigger clients.
And what happened was they took proactive stance.

They got plenty of notice that it was coming and they took proactive stance and just went out and marketed the hell out of the SaaS business part of it, because historically the business wasn't really a SaaS business.
It was more based on subscriptions for their services over the sort of software that they've been building over the last two or three years.
But they have had a big chunk of wins and they've actually sent their new business pipeline over to us.
And I think they've got 129 new opportunities in there, and some of those are already closed and closing as well in the hundreds of thousands.
So the business is certainly in a different place than when you last looked at it.
So, yeah, I mean, I'm kind of excited, really, to open up the data room to give you access to the latest financials.

And if you guys are keen as well, just to have an update meeting with Stuart and Matt and have a discussion about where they are, I think even just in terms of the software, it's moved forwards as well.
So, yeah, some big changes and keen to get you guys back in the process as quick as possible.

I'd be interested to understand how long you guys take to do acquisitions, because we are obviously at the tail end of a process and I want to make sure that we get everything to you as quickly as possible so we can get offers as quickly as possible.
Yeah, okay.
Yeah, that's a good point.
We.
We move at the pace that the sellers want us to.
So typical deal process would take eight weeks, but we do all of our financial diligence, tech diligence in house, so we can move really quickly in that regard.
And if there's an SBA that's been floated around, we can incorporate.

We usually would like to use our own as a starting point because we've done so many deals and it standardizes for us, but we can definitely take uplift what's been agreed and to the best of our ability, to reflect that in our first draft, which would hopefully streamline some of that process.
So realistically, we could get an LOI out once looking at the information and having a meeting with the sellers again, probably could get an LOI out, find a back end of next week.

And just because I wouldn't say the end of this or start towards the start of next week, but just with leave and holidays, it might not be achievable, but then we can probably, on the diligence process, we can go straight away and can be done in six weeks.

I think that in the interest of efficiency, when we were looking for the information, if you can give us a steer on valuation guidance of where they're currently sitting, broadly, like numbers and structures that are attractive to the sellers, that can mean that we make sure that we're coming into a level that is meaningful and we're not wasting anyone's time and making sure that we're being as efficient as possible.
Just on the set, on the customer that left.
Was that Iceland?
It was, yeah.
Okay.
And you mentioned how they've got strong pipeline.
Can you touch on why Iceland left?
I can't give you the exact details.
I think the cycle of the contract had run its course basically.
Okay, is that a deal breaker for you with the connection with Iceland being lost?
No, it's not a deal breaker.
We would definitely want to understand why they've left and to what Sarah's point was before we do look at businesses with strong gross retention.
So like part of our initial analysis will be looking at revenue by customer, historically, hopefully by product.
So we can strip out like understand the SaaS services and commission component to assess those separately but also on a consolidated basis.
And if there have been historical trends of losing significant customers, that would probably raise a pretty significant red flag for us.
But if this is an isolated case where we can understand from management, maybe they've gone to an in house solution or whatever it is, we can work with them on that and take a view.
It's not a deal breaker as long as it's not occurring throughout the whole customer base.
Yeah, no it's not.
I mean it's.
I think it's the other way around, if anything.

So they did have Iceland leave, but they are out in the market up against one other significant other and what they're seeing is a trend where the clients of that other sort of SaaS product that's in the market, which was acquired I think about two years ago.
By next 15 they are losing customers or certainly interest to TSG.
So they're being approached by their customers because TSG's offer is better and these guys haven't responded to customer needs.
So yeah, I think Iceland very much is just an isolated case.
I mean I've got the pipeline up in front of me and is a global pipeline.
They've just won a big contract in Australia as well, just as a sideline.
But it's in Australia, in Europe, across the uk, across the Nordics, South America.
They've got three landing in Uruguay, five landing in Uruguay, Ecuador, Panama, Argentina and then yeah, the rest is a mix of UK and Australia as well.
So they've got a really good strong global pipeline being built.
Yeah, that's very impressive.
I thought there was some New Zealand clients in there, which was a real game changer for me.

I'll have to make sure I get stuck into that during DD on the process standpoint, how far through that when you anticipate to close just so we can be conscious of that and you know, we'll take your lead on what you need and when and do our best to kind of work to that.
You're bang on the timelines.
Actually we were kind of looking to get offers in by the end of this month and then we're keen to get everything done and dusted before the end of August.
I don't know about you guys but for us August is kind of a no man's land.
So we've got a ton of time on our hands to get deals closed.
So yeah, I mean certainly if we could get offers by the end of next week that would be great.
We have a couple of other sort of sizeable, as fleet footed as what you guys sound like.
They've got layers of boards, investment boards that we have to go through.
So they are somewhat slow.

So yeah, my hope is that you guys can beat them to the punch really and just get an offer in because like I say they've been fairly slow I think in terms of being able to feed back to you where they are in valuation because originally I think we went out to market way too high.
It was kind of San Francisco style multiples.
I don't if you saw that on the listing on our agency co website but I think we're in a much more realistic place than the pricing originally.
But I can definitely get a steal from them.
Steer, sorry from them where they would like to get a deal done quickly at and feed that bit back to you.

So they've got a big ambitious sort of goals to hit going forward and they want to get John off the cap table and work within a larger business.
So John's very keen to get a deal done quickly and that will affect pricing as well.
Yeah.

Just help me out.

I don't have it off the top of my head but certainly I could get that to you.
Hey, it's fine.
I'm just.

Just board meetings.

I mean he's very ambitious for what he's built.
Yeah, great.

So I mean my feeling on this is just to get the dd.

summary.overview:
- Capital A and Banyan Software discussed renewed interest in TSG acquisition despite previous decline, with key representatives including Sarah Joel and Andrew Day leading the conversation.  
- Banyan operates 84 portfolio companies, targeting $2-30M annual turnover firms with over 90% gross customer retention, emphasizing decentralized management.  
- TSG expanded its pipeline significantly, now with 129 opportunities, following the exit of Iceland as a major client in mid-2024.  
- Banyan aims for target offers by the end of the month, with a total deal process of 6-8 weeks, potentially closing before August 2024 to avoid seasonal slowdowns.  
- Valuation expectations shifted to realistic levels from previously high San Francisco-style multiples, with ownership equally split among key stakeholders.  
- Banyan shows flexibility on deal structure, offering options for upfront cash or earn-out components, depending on seller preferences.  
- TSG's competitive advantage is growing as a Next15-acquired competitor loses customers due to superior offerings and responsiveness.  
- Historical customer retention analysis is necessary, particularly to assess impact following the departure of Iceland.  
- Ongoing discussions highlight the urgency of preparations, with Banyan's commitment to deliver a Letter of Intent by next week.  
- The meeting underscored Banyan's potential timing advantage over other buyers with slower board approval processes.
summary.short_summary: Capital A and Banyan Software engaged in discussions regarding a renewed interest in the acquisition of TSG, shifting from previous hesitations. Leading the conversation were Sarah Joel and Andrew Day, who outlined Banyan's operational capacity of managing 84 portfolio companies with substantial gross customer retention rates. TSG has expanded its pipeline to 129 opportunities, particularly after the exit of Iceland as a client. Banyan plans to present target offers by the end of the month and aims for a deal closure within 6-8 weeks to avoid seasonal slowdowns. Valuation expectations have moderated to realistic levels, with stakeholders equally sharing ownership. Banyan is flexible in deal structures, accommodating sellers' preferences regarding cash or earn-out options. The urgency of the discussions is highlighted by Banyan's commitment to deliver a Letter of Intent soon, positioning itself advantageously against competitors with slower approval processes.
